idiom_name: entity key member (std::optional<Key>) plus mapper class
implementation_notes: In C++ the classic structure is written by hand: the referencing class holds the target's identity (an integer or strong typedef member, std::optional<Key> when the reference is nullable) and a mapper or repository translates rows to objects, resolving the key to a reference only when the association is needed. Nothing in the standard library provides an ORM, so the mapping layer is yours; the hand-written form stays justified where the schema is legacy or unconstrained, where the domain model must not carry persistence annotations, or when only a few associations need mapping.
pitfalls: std::optional<Key> separates 'no reference' from 'reference to key 0', but a default-constructed Key silently means 'no such row' if the optional is dropped.
Storing the target by reference or pointer inside the entity creates dangling references on copy/move; store the key and resolve through a repository.
A process-global identity map keeps stale objects alive and leaks across sessions; give the cache the lifetime of one unit of work.

variants.name: ODB object relationship (generated mapper)
variants.implementation_notes: ODB inverts the manual approach: persistent classes declare their members and relationships with #pragma directives, and the ODB compiler generates the mapping code and the schema, so the foreign key column and its resolution are produced rather than written. Choose it where the ODB compiler is acceptable in the build and the object model may carry pragmas; the hand-written mapper remains the default when it is not.
pitfalls: The generated schema is a build artifact: change the pragma and the column quietly disappears, so migrations and application code must be regenerated together.
Relationships default to eagerly loaded unless the member is marked as a pointer/lazy where the profile supports it; an accidental eager graph is a join explosion.
